details:
**Ferdinand and Isabella**
The "Catholic Monarchs," Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, whose 1469 marriage united the crowns of Castile and Aragon and laid the foundation of the Spanish state. They completed the Reconquista, established the Spanish Inquisition, and sponsored Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage.

**Reconquista and the fall of Granada (1492)**
The centuries-long Christian campaign to retake the Iberian Peninsula from Muslim rule, traditionally dated from the Battle of Covadonga in 722 (where Pelagius halted the Muslim advance) to 1492. Key moments include the Christian victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 and the 1492 conquest of Granada, after which the last Nasrid ruler, Boabdil, left the Alhambra palace and passed into exile at the spot called "the Moor's Last Sigh."

**Alhambra Decree**
The 1492 edict of Ferdinand and Isabella that expelled from Spain all Jews who refused to convert to Christianity, sending the Sephardic Jews into exile. It is named after the Alhambra, the Nasrid palace in Granada where it was signed.

**Philip II and the Spanish Armada**
Philip II ruled Spain at the height of its power, married Mary I of England, and in 1580 also took the throne of Portugal, creating the Iberian Union. In 1588 he sent the Spanish Armada to invade England; it was defeated at the Battle of Gravelines and scattered by storms. Francis Drake had earlier raided the Spanish fleet at Cádiz.

**Spanish Civil War and Francisco Franco**
The 1936–1939 war in which Francisco Franco's Nationalists defeated the Republicans and installed a dictatorship that lasted until Franco's death in 1975. Associated clues include the Falange party founded by José Antonio Primo de Rivera, the American volunteer Abraham Lincoln Brigade, the "Moscow Gold" shipped from Spain's reserves to the USSR, and the bombing of Guernica by the German Condor Legion. After Franco died, King Juan Carlos oversaw Spain's transition to democracy.

**Al-Andalus and the Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba**
The Muslim name for Iberia after Tariq ibn Ziyad's invasion in 711 overthrew the Visigothic Kingdom. Abd al-Rahman I, an Umayyad prince who escaped the Abbasid takeover, founded the Emirate of Córdoba, which later became a caliphate. After the caliphate collapsed in 1031 amid civil war, it broke into small taifa kingdoms, which were later ruled by the North African Almoravid and Almohad dynasties.

**Eighty Years' War (Dutch Revolt)**
The revolt of the Low Countries against Spanish Habsburg rule, led by William the Silent. Philip II sent the Duke of Alba to suppress it after the Beeldenstorm (iconoclastic riots), and Alba set up the Council of Troubles, nicknamed the "Council of Blood." Spanish troops reached Flanders along the military route called the "Spanish Road," which ran from Milan through Savoy and Lorraine.

**Charles V (Charles I of Spain)**
The Habsburg king of Spain and Holy Roman Emperor who kept his mother, Joanna the Mad, confined, sponsored Magellan's circumnavigation, and defeated France at Pavia in 1525 with infantry formations called tercios. His reliance on Flemish advisors helped spark the Revolt of the Comuneros, and he abdicated in 1556, partly because of painful gout, leaving Spain to his son Philip II.

**Treaty of Tordesillas and Inter caetera**
In the 1493 papal bull Inter caetera, Pope Alexander VI divided newly discovered lands between Spain and Portugal. The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas moved the dividing line of longitude westward, giving Portugal Brazil and Spain most of the rest of the Americas. A later dispute over the Moluccas was settled by the Treaty of Zaragoza, and Francis I of France mocked the division by asking to be shown "Adam's will."

**Valladolid debate and the Spanish Empire in the Americas**
The 1550–1551 debate over the treatment of Native Americans between Bartolomé de las Casas, who defended them, and Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, who justified their conquest. Related clues include the 1542 New Laws protecting natives, the royal "fifth" (quinto real) tax on precious metals, the silver mines of Potosí and Zacatecas, and the conquistadors who toppled the Aztecs and Incas.

**War of the Spanish Succession**
The war (1701–1714) set off when the childless, badly inbred Charles II died, ending Habsburg rule in Spain. It included the Battle of Blenheim and Queen Anne's War in North America, and it ended with the Bourbon Philip V keeping the Spanish throne by renouncing his claim to France, while Britain gained the asiento (a contract to supply slaves to Spanish America).

**Spanish Inquisition**
The tribunal Ferdinand and Isabella established in 1478 to enforce Catholic orthodoxy, especially against converted Jews and Muslims suspected of secretly keeping their old faiths. It held public penance and execution ceremonies called autos-da-fé.

**Peninsular War, the Constitution of 1812, and Ferdinand VII**
During the Napoleonic Wars, Napoleon forced Ferdinand VII to abdicate, and the Cortes of Cádiz wrote the liberal Constitution of 1812. After his restoration, Ferdinand's absolutism provoked the Trienio Liberal (1820–1823), which was crushed by a French army called the "Hundred Thousand Sons of Saint Louis." Meanwhile, Spain lost most of its American colonies to independence movements led by Simón Bolívar.

**Carlist Wars and Isabella II**
A series of 19th-century civil wars in which supporters of Don Carlos, Ferdinand VII's brother, fought the claim of Ferdinand's daughter Isabella II. The Affair of the Spanish Marriages (1846) involved Anglo-French rivalry over whom Isabella and her sister would marry. After the 1868 Glorious Revolution deposed Isabella, the throne was offered to the Prussian prince Leopold of Hohenzollern, sparking the Franco-Prussian War, and the short-reigning Amadeo abdicated in 1873.

**Spanish-American War and the USS Maine**
The 1898 war that followed the explosion of the USS Maine in Havana Harbor, which the American press blamed on Spain. Spain lost, and in the Treaty of Paris it gave up Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines.
